items.stem: This is Secretary of State Charles Evans Hughes, the central American figure at the Washington Naval Conference. Why does the review make Hughes, rather than President Harding, the main actor in the disarmament story?

stimulus.image_caption: Charles Evans Hughes, Secretary of State, in an official portrait (Library of Congress).
stimulus.pd_rationale: Official portrait, Library of Congress; published before 1930, Public domain per Wikimedia Commons license tag

options: (A) Hughes conceived and drove the disarmament diplomacy
(B) Harding publicly opposed holding the conference
(C) The Constitution gives the Secretary of State sole power to make treaties
(D) Hughes later became president and rewrote the history
items.explanation: The review credits Hughes with the conference's dramatic move — stunning delegates by offering to scrap American ships under construction — making him the diplomat who shaped the outcome.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The scrapping proposal that defined the conference was Hughes's initiative.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Harding's administration convened the conference; the president did not oppose it.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Treaties require Senate consent; the Secretary of State has no such sole power.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Hughes never became president; he later served as Chief Justice.

items.fact_source: u7.md §Added 2026-10-01 The Washington Naval Conference (1921–22) — Secretary of State Charles Evans Hughes convened the Washington Naval Conference, where he stunned delegates by proposing the United States scrap ships already under construction

items.stem: The review judges the Good Neighbor Policy a success: U.S.–Latin American relations were better on the eve of World War II than they had been in decades. What best explains the improvement?
options: (A) The United States increased its military occupations in the region
(B) Ending the occupations removed the main source of resentment
(C) Latin American nations adopted the Roosevelt Corollary themselves
(D) The Great Depression ended in 1933
items.explanation: Resentment had been caused by the occupations and the claimed right to intervene; removing both removed the grievance, which is why relations improved.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The occupations were wound down, not increased.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Non-intervention took away what Latin Americans had resented.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The Corollary was the American claim Latin America opposed; no one adopted it.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The Depression continued through the 1930s; the improvement came from the policy change.

items.fact_source: u7.md §Added 2026-10-01 The Good Neighbor Policy (1930s) — it worked: U.S.-Latin American relations were better on the eve of World War II than they had been in decades

items.stem: The Nye Committee concluded that arms makers and bankers had dragged America into World War I. What did Congress conclude from this finding?
options: (A) The United States should join the League of Nations
(B) The arms makers should be put in charge of foreign policy
(C) The United States should declare war earlier in the next European conflict
(D) Economic ties caused the entanglement, so law must cut those ties
items.explanation: If business ties caused the war entry, the remedy was legal separation: the Neutrality Acts embargoed arms and banned loans to belligerents.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The finding pushed Congress toward neutrality laws, not toward the League.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The Committee blamed the arms makers; Congress did not reward them.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The entire point was to avoid the next war, not to enter it sooner.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The diagnosis (economic entanglement) dictated the prescription (legal bans on arms and loans).

items.fact_source: u7.md §Added 2026-10-01 The Neutrality Acts (1935–37) — Congress passed a series of Neutrality Acts driven by the Nye Committee's finding that arms makers and bankers had dragged America into World War I

items.stem: The review argues the Neutrality Acts rested on a misreading of 1917: German submarines, not economic ties, had caused the American war declaration. What follows from this judgment?
options: (A) The Nye Committee's premise was correct after all
(B) Submarines played no role in the First World War
(C) Economic ties were the true cause of the 1917 war declaration
(D) The laws attacked the wrong cause
items.explanation: If unrestricted submarine warfare caused the declaration, then cutting off arms sales and loans — the Neutrality Acts' remedy — attacked a cause that had not decided the matter.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The review explicitly calls the premise a misreading.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The review says submarines were the cause; they plainly played a role.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. This restates the Nye premise the review rejects.
option_explanations.D: Correct. A remedy aimed at the wrong cause cannot prevent the outcome.

items.fact_source: u7.md §Added 2026-10-01 The Neutrality Acts (1935–37) — the legislation rested on a misreading of 1917: economic ties hadn't caused the war declaration; German submarines had

items.stem: The 1937 Neutrality Act let belligerents buy non-military goods only if they paid cash and carried the goods away in their own ships. Though written impartially, why did "cash-and-carry" help Britain and France?

stimulus.text: The 1937 act added "cash-and-carry," letting belligerents buy non-military goods only if they paid cash and carried them in their own ships.

options: (A) British and French sea power meant only they could carry goods away
(B) They were the only countries in the world holding any cash reserves
(C) The act named Britain and France as its preferred buyers
(D) Germany possessed no merchant ships of its own at all
items.explanation: Impartial rules applied to unequal powers produce unequal results: the sea-lane advantage meant cash-and-carry was usable by Britain and France but not by Germany.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Control of the seas decided who could actually use the provision.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Many countries held cash; the constraint was carrying the goods, not paying for them.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The act was written to treat all belligerents alike; it named no favorites.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Germany had merchant shipping; the problem was getting it past British and French naval control.

items.fact_source: u7.md §Added 2026-10-01 The Neutrality Acts (1935–37) — cash-and-carry in practice helped Britain and France, which controlled the sea lanes; neutrality failed because impartiality favors the strong

items.stem: Roosevelt chipped away at the Neutrality Acts — repealing the arms embargo in 1939 and winning Lend-Lease in 1941 — and Pearl Harbor ended the experiment. What does this arc from 1935 to 1941 show?
options: (A) American isolationism grew steadily stronger through 1941
(B) The isolationist peak receded as war neared
(C) Roosevelt remained a lifelong supporter of the Neutrality Acts throughout
(D) Pearl Harbor had no effect whatsoever on the neutrality laws
items.explanation: The sequence runs from the Acts' passage to their erosion to their end: the isolationist peak passed as the world crisis deepened, carrying America toward its postwar global role.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The repeal and Lend-Lease show isolationism weakening, not strengthening.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The arc is the bridge the review describes between 1930s neutrality and post-1941 globalism.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Roosevelt worked to undo the Acts, not to preserve them.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Pearl Harbor ended the neutrality experiment outright.

items.fact_source: u7.md §Added 2026-10-01 The Neutrality Acts (1935–37) — Roosevelt chipped away at the laws (repealing the arms embargo in 1939, Lend-Lease in 1941), and Pearl Harbor ended the experiment; the isolationist impulse's high-water mark, and the bridge between the 1930s and America's post-1941 globalism

items.stem: This 1846 daguerreotype shows Ralph Waldo Emerson, whose 1841 essay "Self-Reliance" declared: "Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string." According to the transcendentalists, where does truth come from?

stimulus.pd_rationale: 1846 daguerreotype; pre-1930 work, Public domain per Wikimedia Commons license tag

options: (A) From the doctrine of the church alone
(B) From the great philosophers of Europe alone
(C) From self-trust and nature, not institutions
(D) From the laws passed by the government
items.explanation: Emerson's creed, as the review summarizes it, located truth in the individual: self-trust and direct experience of nature outranked churches, parties, and inherited tradition.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The transcendentalists held that institutions, including churches, corrupted the individual.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Emerson urged Americans to stop imitating Europe, not to follow its philosophers.
option_explanations.C: Correct. "Trust thyself" is the doctrine: the individual, not the institution, is the source of truth.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Government law was among the institutions the transcendentalists distrusted.

items.fact_source: u4.md §Added 2026-10-01 Transcendentalism — truth came from self-trust and direct experience of nature rather than tradition; Emerson's 1841 essay "Self-Reliance": "Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string"

items.stem: This 1856 daguerreotype shows Henry David Thoreau. After spending a night in jail for refusing a poll tax during the Mexican War, he argued that conscience outranks law — an argument later abolitionists and civil-rights activists cited. What does that later citation show?

stimulus.pd_rationale: 1856 daguerreotype by Benjamin D. Maxham; pre-1930 work, Public domain per Wikimedia Commons license tag

options: (A) Thoreau personally led the later civil-rights movement
(B) The Mexican War ended because of his essay
(C) Poll taxes were abolished in 1849
(D) His principle outlived its moment and served later causes
items.explanation: An 1849 argument about a poll tax was still being cited a century later: the idea proved portable across reform movements and generations.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Thoreau died in 1862; later activists cited his writing, he did not lead them.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The war ended for military and diplomatic reasons, not because of the essay.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Poll taxes persisted long after 1849.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The citation history shows the principle's long afterlife in American reform.

items.fact_source: u4.md §Added 2026-10-01 Transcendentalism — his 1849 essay on civil disobedience, written after he spent a night in jail for refusing a poll tax during the Mexican War, argued that conscience outranks law, a principle later abolitionists and civil-rights activists would cite

items.stem: The review stresses that transcendentalism "never was" a mass movement. A student concludes the movement was therefore historically unimportant. What is the best evaluation?
options: (A) Ideas matter more than membership: the circle fueled three reform movements
(B) The student is right, since only mass movements have ever mattered in all of history
(C) Transcendentalism actually counted millions of members
(D) Emerson and his circle actively opposed all of the reform movements
items.explanation: The review's whole point is that influence and membership are different measures: a small circle's ideas — individual self-trust applied to reform — powered causes far larger than the circle itself.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The movement matters as the intellectual fuel of the reform era, not as a mass organization.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Ideas from small groups have repeatedly shaped mass movements.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The review explicitly says it never was a mass movement.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The circle's confidence in individual remaking powered the era's reforms.

items.fact_source: u4.md §Added 2026-10-01 Transcendentalism — transcendentalism matters for the exam not as a mass movement, it never was one, but as the intellectual fuel of the reform era; the same confidence that the individual could remake himself powered temperance, abolitionism, and women's rights

items.stem: This 1846 daguerreotype shows Margaret Fuller, a member of Emerson's circle. Her Woman in the Nineteenth Century (1845) fed the Seneca Falls generation. What does this link show?

stimulus.pd_rationale: 1846 daguerreotype by John Plumbe, Jr.; pre-1930 work, Public domain per Wikimedia Commons license tag

options: (A) Fuller personally organized the Seneca Falls convention
(B) Transcendentalist ideas fed the women's rights movement
(C) Emerson personally opposed the cause of women's rights
(D) Fuller's book was published after Seneca Falls met
items.explanation: Fuller's book carried the circle's confidence in individual self-remaking into the argument for women's rights, feeding the generation that met at Seneca Falls in 1848.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The review says her book fed the Seneca Falls generation; Stanton and Mott organized the convention.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The link shows ideas traveling from the transcendentalist circle into women's rights.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Fuller was in Emerson's circle; nothing in the review suggests his opposition.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The book appeared in 1845, three years before Seneca Falls.

items.fact_source: u4.md §Added 2026-10-01 Transcendentalism — Emerson's circle included Margaret Fuller, whose 1845 Woman in the Nineteenth Century fed the Seneca Falls generation
